junction.name: East 149 Street & Melrose Avenue, New York City

claims.text: East 149 Street & Melrose Avenue had 88 injury crashes in police records since 2021-10-31: 37 pedestrians injured, 15 cyclists injured and 1 person killed.
At the U.S. DOT's values that harm costs about $6.0 million a year.
27% of crashes here involved a two-wheeler, against 16% at the city's priority junctions.
2% of crashes here had “failure to yield to an emergency vehicle” recorded as a contributing factor, against 0% at the city's priority junctions.

Held up on later years: a vehicle was going straight ahead and a two-wheeler was involved in 27% of crashes since 2024-05-01, against 14% at the city's priority junctions (found by the AI analyst and the greedy search).

The city's Leading Pedestrian Interval signals: passed the causal gate (pedestrian injury crashes changed -17% (95% interval -22% to -11%) at 1,651 sites against sites treated later or the citywide trend, and a placebo date shows nothing).
The city's turn traffic calming: earlier trend (a simple before/after says -26%, but a placebo date before the work shows a drop too, so the decline cannot be credited to the program).
The city's enhanced crossings: not shown (at 96 sites the change in pedestrian injury crashes (-7%, 95% interval -50% to +69%) could be zero).
The city's speed humps: not shown (at 1,008 sites the change in injury crashes (+0%, 95% interval -9% to +9%) could be zero).
Backplates with Retroreflective Borders would avoid about 2.6 crashes a year (CMF 1410, the record FHWA's fact sheet cites; evidence: the record FHWA cites), worth $904,000 a year.

Yellow Change Intervals would avoid about 1.4 crashes a year (CMF 4219, the more conservative of the two middle records of 4; evidence: only if a site check confirms it), worth $470,000 a year; check on site: the current yellow plus all-red time is below the ITE recommended practice.
The NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) is responsible for East 149 Street, Melrose Avenue (not listed in NYSDOT Roadway Inventory, so a city street).
Who can push for it: Council Member, District 17, New York City Council; Bronx Community Board 1.
A request letter to the NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) is drafted and checked.

draft_request.letter:
To: the NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT)
Cc: Council Member, District 17, New York City Council; Bronx Community Board 1
Subject: Request for safety review at East 149 Street & Melrose Avenue

Dear colleagues at NYC DOT,

We are writing about the junction of East 149 Street & Melrose Avenue, for which you are responsible for East 149 Street and Melrose Avenue.

The official record for the 5 years from 31 October 2021 shows 176 crashes, including 88 injury crashes, with 37 pedestrians and 15 cyclists injured and 1 person killed. This junction is flagged as a city priority location. By the U.S. DOT's official values for the cost of crashes (2024 dollars), the harm is about 6.0 million dollars per year. The record shows no recorded safety treatment in this period; the most recent recorded project was a Leading Pedestrian Interval signal in 2019.

We ask you to carry out a safety study at this junction and, on the roads you control, to assess the following low-cost fixes:

* longer yellow signal times, which are expected to prevent about 4.8 injury crashes per year, avoiding about $1,639,000 in harm per year;
* reflective backplates on the traffic signals, which are expected to prevent about 2.6 injury crashes per year, avoiding about $904,000 in harm per year.

Please check on site whether each measure suits the layout and signals, and proceed where appropriate.

Thank you for your attention to safety at this junction.

[Your name]
[Your organisation or address]
